Root read its complete argument and the bound primary text of Friedland–Yomdin arXiv:1503.00325v1 Example 1.1 and the target arXiv:1909.04918v1 Section 4. The earlier example supplies the family h(x)=x+x^N for every N>=11. For t>=2, set p=3^t, N=pt+1, and f(z)=h(3z)/3. Then f=z+3^(pt)z^(pt+1). The initial coefficient maximum through cutoff p is one, and its only nonzero tail coefficient is 3^(pt)=p^p<=N^p. Its N distinct simple zeros consist of zero and the N-1 roots of z^(N-1)=-3^(-(N-1)), all at modulus 1/3. Thus its zero-count/cutoff ratio is t+1/p, unbounded. This verifies every hypothesis of the fixed-C=1, fixed-radius question; it does not transport the older example's small-disc valency theorem across incompatible discs.

**1. Friedland–Goldman–Yomdin, 1909.04918v1, Section 4 example 2 p9; Definition 1.1 p2.** For every C>0, does there exist K(C)<infinity such that for every integer p>=1 and every analytic f(z)=sum a_k z^k with radius>1 satisfying |a_k|<=C k^p max_(0<=i<=p)|a_i| for every integer k>=p+1, f takes each complex value at most K(C)p times in |z|<1/2? **Complete ordinary refutation at C=1**, offered for review in PROOF.md. For t>=1, p=3^t, m=pt, f=z+3^m z^(m+1) has domination and pt+1 distinct half-disc zeros. Independent real-rooted product construction also refutes it. No inspected theorem gives the lower witness or linear fixed-radius endpoint. **HOLD**: bounded history/title/author search found no exact prior resolution, but old sharpness literature and live proof registries are not cleared.
